concepts.name: Definition and Core Mechanism of Cost-Push Inflation
key_dimensions: Supply-side origin vs. demand-side origin: distinguishing cost-push from demand-pull
Role of rising production costs in shifting the aggregate supply (AS) curve leftward
Stagflation trap: simultaneous rise in inflation and unemployment unique to cost-push
UPSC trap: cost-push can occur even when aggregate demand is stagnant or falling

concepts.name: Wage-Price Spiral as a Trigger of Cost-Push Inflation
key_dimensions: Mechanism: higher wages → higher production costs → higher prices → demand for higher wages
Role of trade unions and collective bargaining in initiating the spiral
Distinction from demand-pull: wage increase here is a supply shock, not a demand stimulus
Policy dilemma: suppressing wages vs. controlling inflation without hurting workers

concepts.name: Oil Price Shock as a Classic Cost-Push Trigger
key_dimensions: Historical context: 1973 OPEC oil embargo and 1979 oil crisis as textbook examples
Transmission mechanism: oil → transport, manufacturing, agriculture input costs → general price rise
India-specific vulnerability: India imports ~85% of its crude oil, making it highly susceptible
UPSC trap: oil shock affects both WPI (directly) and CPI (indirectly via transport and food)

concepts.name: Raw Material and Commodity Price Shocks
key_dimensions: Global commodity cycles (metals, minerals, agricultural inputs) and their pass-through to domestic prices
India's import dependence on commodities like coal, edible oils, fertilizers, and semiconductors
Distinction between tradable and non-tradable sectors in absorbing commodity shocks
UPSC trap: rise in global commodity prices is an external cost-push factor beyond RBI's control

concepts.name: Supply Chain Disruptions as a Modern Cost-Push Source
key_dimensions: COVID-19 pandemic as a contemporary case study of global supply chain-induced cost-push inflation
Just-in-time inventory model vulnerability and its inflationary consequences
Semiconductor shortage (2020–2022) and its cascading effect on automobile and electronics prices
Policy limitation: monetary tightening cannot resolve supply chain bottlenecks

concepts.name: Agricultural Supply Shocks and Food Inflation in India
key_dimensions: Monsoon failure, floods, and pest attacks as cost-push triggers specific to India's food economy
Structural bottlenecks: poor storage (cold chain), APMC inefficiencies raising cost of farm-to-market
Distinction: food inflation in India is often supply-driven (cost-push) not demand-driven
UPSC trap: RBI's flexible inflation targeting (FIT) framework targets CPI which has ~46% food weight — monetary policy has limited efficacy against food cost-push inflation

concepts.name: Energy Price Transmission: Fuel, Electricity, and Natural Gas
key_dimensions: How administered fuel prices in India (petrol, diesel under dynamic pricing; LPG, kerosene under subsidy) modulate cost-push transmission
Electricity tariff revisions by State Electricity Regulatory Commissions as a cost-push source for industry
Natural gas price hikes affecting fertilizer production costs and consequently food prices
UPSC trap: deregulation of fuel prices increases cost-push inflation pass-through but improves fiscal health

concepts.name: Tax and Regulatory Cost as Government-Induced Cost-Push Inflation
key_dimensions: Excise duty, GST rate hikes, and customs tariffs increasing input costs for producers
Environmental regulations (pollution norms, carbon taxes) raising compliance costs — 'green inflation'
Minimum Wage Act revisions and their inflationary impact on labor-intensive sectors
UPSC trap: government-induced cost-push is a policy variable — it is controllable but politically sensitive

concepts.name: Exchange Rate Depreciation and Imported Inflation
key_dimensions: Mechanism: rupee depreciation → costlier imports → higher input costs for domestic producers
Key import categories vulnerable: crude oil, fertilizers, edible oils, capital goods
Distinction between imported inflation (cost-push) and domestic demand inflation
UPSC trap: RBI's forex intervention to stabilize the rupee is partly an anti-cost-push inflation tool, but it depletes forex reserves

concepts.name: Stagflation: The Defining Macroeconomic Outcome of Cost-Push Inflation
key_dimensions: Definition: simultaneous occurrence of high inflation, high unemployment, and low/negative growth
Why stagflation cannot be solved by conventional monetary or fiscal policy alone
1970s global stagflation vs. 2022 post-COVID stagflation fears as case studies
UPSC trap: demand-pull inflation does NOT cause stagflation; only cost-push or supply shocks do

concepts.name: Phillips Curve Breakdown Under Cost-Push Inflation
key_dimensions: Original Phillips Curve: inverse trade-off between inflation and unemployment (demand-side logic)
Cost-push inflation causes an outward shift of the short-run Phillips Curve — both inflation and unemployment rise simultaneously
Stagflation of the 1970s empirically disproved the stable Phillips Curve relationship
UPSC trap: Phillips Curve trade-off is valid for demand-pull inflation but NOT for cost-push inflation

concepts.name: Monetary Policy Response to Cost-Push Inflation: Effectiveness and Limitations
key_dimensions: Rate hike mechanism: raises borrowing costs, suppresses demand — but does not address the supply-side cause
Risk of policy error: aggressive rate hikes during cost-push inflation can deepen recession without resolving inflation
RBI's dilemma: inflation above 6% (upper tolerance band) mandates action even if supply-driven
UPSC trap: monetary policy is the primary tool for demand-pull inflation but is blunt and potentially harmful for cost-push inflation

concepts.name: Supply-Side Policy Responses to Cost-Push Inflation
key_dimensions: Investment in infrastructure to reduce logistics and supply chain costs (PM Gati Shakti, NIP)
Reducing import dependence: domestic production of fertilizers, solar panels, semiconductors
Agricultural reforms: better MSP logistics, cold chain, contract farming to stabilize food supply
UPSC trap: supply-side responses are structurally correct but time-lagged — they cannot provide immediate inflation relief

concepts.name: Fiscal Policy Tools to Counter Cost-Push Inflation
key_dimensions: Reducing indirect taxes (excise duty cuts on fuel in 2022 by Indian government) to lower consumer prices
Subsidies on key inputs (fertilizer subsidy, LPG subsidy) to absorb cost-push pressure
Trade policy: reducing import duties on essential commodities to increase supply (e.g., edible oil import duty cuts)
UPSC trap: fiscal measures to counter cost-push inflation (subsidies, tax cuts) worsen fiscal deficit, creating another macroeconomic risk

concepts.name: Cost-Push Inflation vs. Demand-Pull Inflation: Key Differentiators
key_dimensions: Origin: supply side (AS shift left) vs. demand side (AD shift right)
Output effect: cost-push reduces output; demand-pull increases output (at least in the short run)
Policy prescription differs fundamentally: supply-side reform vs. demand compression
UPSC trap: both cause rising prices but have opposite effects on GDP and employment — a favorite MCQ trap

concepts.name: Cost-Push Inflation and the WPI–CPI Divergence in India
key_dimensions: WPI captures prices at the producer/wholesale level — more directly reflects input cost shocks
CPI captures retail-level prices — includes services and food, affected by both cost-push and demand factors
High WPI with moderate CPI may indicate cost-push inflation being absorbed by producers (margin compression)
UPSC trap: RBI targets CPI (not WPI) for monetary policy under FIT — a cost-push shock showing up in WPI may not immediately trigger RBI action

concepts.name: Core vs. Headline Inflation Distinction in the Context of Cost-Push
key_dimensions: Headline CPI includes food and fuel — both highly vulnerable to cost-push shocks
Core inflation (CPI excluding food and fuel) is less affected by supply shocks and reflects underlying demand pressures
Persistently high core inflation alongside high headline = both demand and supply factors at play
UPSC trap: central banks globally focus on core inflation for policy decisions because food and fuel volatility is considered transitory cost-push

concepts.name: Inflationary Expectations and Second-Round Effects of Cost-Push Inflation
key_dimensions: If cost-push inflation becomes entrenched in expectations, it can trigger wage demands and price hikes even after original shock dissipates
Role of credible central bank communication (forward guidance) in anchoring expectations
RBI's inflation targeting mandate as an expectations management tool
UPSC trap: the second-round effect of cost-push inflation (through expectations) can look like demand-pull inflation, making diagnosis and policy response complex

concepts.name: Climate Change and Structural Cost-Push Inflation ('Climateflation')
key_dimensions: Extreme weather events (droughts, floods, heat waves) destroying crops and raising food prices — a recurring and worsening cost-push source
Carbon pricing and green transition costs raising energy and production costs ('greenflation')
Stranded asset risk in fossil fuel sector creating supply gaps and price spikes
UPSC trap: climate-induced cost-push inflation is a long-term structural challenge that neither monetary nor short-term fiscal policy can adequately address

concepts.name: Geopolitical Shocks as an External Cost-Push Trigger
key_dimensions: Russia–Ukraine war (2022): spike in crude oil, natural gas, wheat, sunflower oil, and fertilizer prices — textbook external cost-push shock
Trade wars and sanctions disrupting supply chains (US–China tech war affecting semiconductor supply)
India's 'friend-shoring' and strategic reserves (Strategic Petroleum Reserve) as buffers against geopolitical cost-push shocks
UPSC trap: geopolitical cost-push shocks are entirely external and beyond domestic monetary policy control — highlights limits of inflation targeting in open economies
